On the readability of long documents

A test article with headings, links, quotations, code and lists, so the minimap has something with real structure and colour to render.

The problem with scrolling

Reading a long document by scrolling is a search problem dressed up as a navigation problem. You know roughly what you want, you move down in blind slices, you stop, you read a little, and you move again. The cost of every iteration is paid whether or not the slice you stopped at contained anything.

A scrollbar that showed the shape of the whole document would change the shape of that search. Instead of choosing a slice and checking it, you could see where you are in the whole and aim. This is the trick text editors have used for thirty years, and it works because the cost of looking is far lower than the cost of guessing.

See the original note or the follow-up discussion for more on the ergonomics.

What the map should show

Enough to recognise structure, not so much that it becomes a document in its own right. A schematic that lists every element is useless, because it has the same information density as the thing it is summarising.

The map should answer one question quickly: is what I am looking for above me, below me, or nowhere near here?

Dense text and sparse text should look different. A heading should be distinguishable from body copy at a glance, without reading it.

Colour as structure

Colour is doing most of the work here. A page already assigns different colours to headings, links, quotations and code, and reusing those is cheaper and more faithful than inventing a palette. A rendered map that is monochrome throws away the one signal the page was already giving us for free.

Implementation notes

Drawing one mark per character, rather than per element, keeps the map honest about density. A paragraph with many short lines and a paragraph with two long ones should not look alike.

for each run of text:
    y = floor(run.top * scale)
    if y == last_row: skip
    for each pixel of width:
        ch = run.text[pixel * step]
        if not ch.isspace(): mark(pixel, y)

The step is what keeps a very long line from being drawn off the edge of the strip, and it is the only part of this that has no direct analogue in a text editor, where lines are usually a known width.

Interaction

  • Hovering the map should preview the text under the cursor.
  • Clicking should move the viewport there, not merely scroll by a page.
  • Dragging should continue smoothly, as a native scrollbar does.

None of this is difficult. It is mostly the discipline of doing the cheap thing on every pointer move, because pointer moves are the one interaction that happens hundreds of times a minute.

Limits

Pages that virtualise their content will not map correctly, because the document has no real height. Pages inside content-visibility: auto are fine, since the text is in the DOM whether or not it has been painted — which is precisely the case that defeats screenshot-based approaches.

The honest summary is that a map is a navigation aid, not a substitute for reading. It tells you where things are. You still have to go and look at them, which is rather the point.
